title: Umar ibn al-Khattab
def: The second caliph (r. 634–644), known for justice, who expanded the state from Egypt to Persia.
what: Umar accepted Islam in Mecca and strengthened the early community. As caliph he took Jerusalem, set up courts and the diwan, and counted the calendar from the Hijra. A famous report has him walking at night to see that the poor were fed. He was killed by a Persian slave in 644. The Prophet called him “al-Faruq”, the one who separates truth from falsehood.

title: Ummah
def: The community of Muslims, united by faith across nations and cultures.
what: The Quran calls the Muslims a “middle” or balanced community (2:143), and says that “this community of yours is one community” (21:92). A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari compares the believers, in their mutual love and mercy, to one body: if one part suffers, the rest respond with sleeplessness and fever.
At the same time the Quran affirms diversity: peoples and tribes were made so that they should come to know one another, and the most honoured is the most God-conscious (49:13).
misread: That the ummah is a political bloc seeking to dominate the world.
sources: The ummah is a community of faith and ethics. Muslims live in states of every kind and have fought and allied with one another and with non-Muslims for every reason. The word is also used in the Quran for other peoples with their own prophets (10:47), which shows it is not a political claim.

title: Ummi
def: The Prophet is called ummī, “unlettered”, and the Quran uses ummiyyūn for the unlettered and for gentiles.
what: “Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered prophet” (7:157). The Quran tells the Prophet: “You did not recite any book before it, nor write it with your right hand; otherwise those who follow falsehood would have doubted” (29:48). The Prophet said: “We are an unlettered nation; we do not write or calculate” (Sahih al-Bukhari), speaking of the Arabs. In 3:75 some of the People of the Book say “there is no blame on us in regard to the ummiyyīn”, a term for those who are not Jews.
misread: That the Prophet could not have known the stories of earlier prophets.
sources: Muslims see the Prophet’s unlettered state as part of the sign of the Quran: it was not a work of a scholar. Some scholars say ummī means “from the Mother of Cities”, Mecca, or “of the nations”, and the sense is not disputed that he had no formal training in scripture.

title: Umrah
def: The lesser pilgrimage, which can be made at any time of year.
what: The rites are ihram, tawaf of the Kaaba, sa‘i between Safa and Marwa and shaving or trimming the hair. Unlike Hajj it is not tied to a date, and is highly recommended; the Prophet said that one umrah to the next expiates what is between (Sahih al-Bukhari).

title: 'Urf, al-
def: The common and approved custom of a people, used in the absence of a contrary ruling as a basis from which law is derived
what: ʿUrf means what is known and approved among people. Jurists accept it as a source of rulings where no text or other source decides the matter. The Quran tells the Prophet to “enjoin what is customary and good” (7:199), and the word there is ʿurf. Custom helps fix matters the texts leave open, such as what counts as reasonable maintenance in a marriage or the usual meaning of a word in a contract. Its limits are clear: a custom that contradicts the Quran or the Sunnah has no force. The jurists’ maxim holds that custom may serve as a basis for judgement.
misread: That custom can override the Quran, when the law accepts custom only where the texts are silent.

title: Usul al-Fiqh
def: The sources of Islamic law: the Quran, the Sunnah, consensus and analogy, together with the principles for using them
what: Uṣūl al-fiqh means the roots of the law. The agreed sources are the Quran, the Sunnah of the Prophet (peace be upon him), the consensus of qualified scholars (ijmāʿ) and analogy (qiyās). Jurists also discuss further principles, such as public interest, custom and presumption of continuity, on which the schools differ. The distinction between the two terms is one of level. Fiqh is the body of rulings, and uṣūl al-fiqh is the set of sources and rules from which the rulings are drawn. Al-Shāfiʿī’s Risālah is the earliest surviving systematic treatment.
misread: That it is the same as fiqh, when it names the sources from which fiqh is derived.

title: Usul Fiqh
def: Islamic jurisprudence: the method of deriving laws from the sources of Islam and of establishing their juristic validity
what: Uṣūl fiqh is the discipline of legal method. It teaches how a ruling is drawn from the Quran, the Sunnah and the other sources, how a command or prohibition is to be read, how an apparent conflict between texts is resolved, and who is qualified to exercise ijtihād. Ismail al-Faruqi presents it as the means by which the validity of a law, both juristic and constitutional, is established. The field has its own literature, with chapters on language, on the weight of evidence and on the effect of general and specific wording. Students study it alongside fiqh, the rulings themselves.
misread: That Islamic law is a fixed list of rules, when it is a method of reasoning from sources.

title: Uswah Hasanah
def: The good and normative example of the Prophet (peace be upon him), whose conduct makes up the sunnah
what: Uswah ḥasanah means a good example. The Quran says: “In the Messenger of Allah you have a good example for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day and remembers Allah often” (33:21). The same expression is used of Abraham and his followers (60:4). Muslims understand the conduct of Muhammad (peace be upon him) as the model for belief, worship and character, and they learn it from hadith and from his biography. The Quran praises him as “of great moral character” (68:4). His example is that of a human being, and it forms the sunnah, the second source of law after the Quran.
misread: That following the Prophet means treating him as divine, when the Quran presents him as a human being who sets an example.
